body:
Correct, this happens if I have set local_resources.  I haven't actually tried it without local_resources set.

I have a bunch of targets which all depend on a library.  When I change the library, it should trigger 20+ links, most of them in parallel.  When I watch what is happening with top, I only see one instance of the linker running at a time.
Maybe @philwo can take a look, since he is about to make a few changes in this area.

Thanks!  One of my suspicions is that the md5sum calculation done after building an artifact is single-threaded in bazel, and this is causing slowdowns for rules quickly generating large outputs.  If there is some sort of trace that would help you, please let me know.

The md5sum calculation is indeed single-threaded. [DigestUtils does it intentionally](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/blob/master/src/main/java/com/google/devtools/build/lib/actions/cache/DigestUtils.java#L117). I can see how that improves performance for HDDs, but it seems like there should be a way to disable or tune it for machines without seek latency.

This also makes SkyframeActionExecutor.checkActionCache with a big output file much slower than necessary on my machine (2 hyperthreaded cores and an SSD) because bazel spends a long time pegging a single core calculating the MD5 of the single large file.

issue.title: Serialized MD5 calls slow down ∅ builds

labels.name: P2
labels.description: We'll consider working on this in future. (Assignee optional)

repository.name: bazel
repository.description: a fast, scalable, multi-language and extensible build system

issue.body:
#1042, #923, and #835 are running into the same problem from different perspectives.  I'm adding this issue for the core problem in Bazel: it serializes hashing artifacts larger than 4K.

Even setting up Bazel for success with no changes at all, Kythe's build is rather slow because of this (we have quite a few large >4K artifacts):

```
$ bazel build //...
INFO: Found 692 targets...
INFO: Elapsed time: 5.564s, Critical Path: 4.66s
```

The suggestion to use `--noexperimental_check_output_file` (from #923) does not improve this situation:

```
bazel build --noexperimental_check_output_file //...
INFO: Found 692 targets...
INFO: Elapsed time: 5.206s, Critical Path: 4.64s
```

However, if I rebuild Bazel to remove the synchronization on the `MD5_LOCK` in `DigestUtils.java`, the null build is much nicer:

```
$ bazel build //...
INFO: Found 692 targets...
INFO: Elapsed time: 1.289s, Critical Path: 0.58s
```

The reasoning for this serialization in `DigestUtils.java` does not seem to universally apply (as stated in #835 and made apparent with the above experiment):

```
// We'll have to read file content in order to calculate the digest. In that case
// it would be beneficial to serialize those calculations since there is a high
// probability that MD5 will be requested for multiple output files simultaneously.
// Exception is made for small (<=4K) files since they will not likely to introduce
// significant delays (at worst they will result in two extra disk seeks by
// interrupting other reads).
```

As for a solution, here's my two cents.  If there is evidence that the serialization does benefit some builds, then I would like to see a flag to adjust this on a per machine case (with `.bazelrc`) or maybe have Bazel figure it out on its own if it can.   If there isn't any evidence that the serialization helps, then perhaps it's time to remove it altogether.

body: Philipp has been looking at making DigestUtils not single-threaded, but it's tricky as long as we need to support hard drives with spinning platters. :-(
Couldn't you replace the mutex with a semaphore which is initialized to the number of IO units?

What are IO units?

The problem is that if you have a spinning platter, single-threading gives you the best performance in some scenarios.

While I personally would like to just get rid of HDD-specific optimizations and I/O accounting, the less extreme proposal would probably be to somehow detect whether the output_base is on an SSD and tune the available I/O units in the Bazel resource management system accordingly (i.e. set to 1 when running on an HDD, set to infinite when running on an SSD).

Then replace the mutex with a semaphore initialized to the number of available I/O, as @AustinSchuh proposed.

I think we should add a short-term workaround, e.g., read an environment variable BAZEL_MULTITHREADED_DIGEST, and use that to either disable the lock or turn it into a semaphore. This isn't a good long-term fix, but at least it would reduce the pain a bit.
I'll send a CL tomorrow that implements a workaround for this.
@AustinSchuh was talking about the IO setting of --local_resources. Seems like using that instead of an environment variable might be a bit nicer to use.

Yes, a flag would be nicer, but unfortunately the lock is very deep in the
bowels of Bazel in a way that makes it hard to pass a flag there. Otherwise
we could try to auto-detect whether it's an ssd or not.
